At the latitude of Sullivan's Island, winters are rarely very harsh, and during the autumn a fire is thought necessary on very few occasions indeed. Towards the middle of October, 18—, however, came a day of unusual cold. A little before sundown I made my scrambling way through the evergreens to my friend's hut; several weeks had passed since my last visit, for I was then living in Charleston, nine miles from the island, and the means of travelling to and fro fell far short of those now available. Arriving at the hut, I knocked according to my habit, and, receiving no answer, looked for the key in its familiar hiding-place, opened the door, and entered. A splendid fire burned on the hearth. The sight was uncommon, and anything but unwelcome. I cast aside my overcoat, settled into an arm-chair beside the snapping logs, and patiently waited for my hosts to return.

They came shortly after nightfall and welcomed me with great warmth. Jupiter, smiling broadly, hurried about getting some marsh-hens ready for supper. Legrand was seized by one of his bouts—what other name can I give them?—of enthusiasm. He had discovered an unfamiliar bivalve constituting a new genus; and, beyond this, with Jupiter's help he had pursued and captured a scarabæus which he supposed entirely unknown, but upon which he desired my judgment the next morning.

“Why not this evening?” I enquired, warming my hands above the flames and wishing the entire tribe of scarabæi to the devil.

“Ah, had I only known you were here!” Legrand answered. “But we have not met for so long; how could I guess you would choose this particular night for a visit? On my way back I encountered Lieutenant G——, of the fort, and was foolish enough to lend him the insect. You cannot possibly see it before morning. Remain here overnight, and I shall send Jup to fetch it at sunrise. It is the most beautiful thing in creation!”

“What is?—the sunrise?”

“Nonsense! Certainly not—the beetle. Its colour is a dazzling gold, and it is about as large as a big hickory-nut, with two coal-black marks near one end of its back, and a third, rather longer, at the opposite end. Its antennæ are—”

“Dere ain't any tin in him, Massa Will, as I keeps tellin you,” Jupiter broke in here. “Dat bug is gold, solid gold, ebery bit, de inside too, all 'cept de wings. I ain't neber held a bug half so hebby in all my life.”

‘Oh, it is nothing! I enjoy it. I do not work for money; my art is my whole life.’

Lord Arthur placed four pounds, two shillings and sixpence on the table and thanked the little German for his kindness. After managing to refuse an invitation to meet some Anarchists over a meal of meat and tea the following Saturday, he left the house and headed for the Park.

For the next two days he was intensely excited. At noon on Friday he drove to the Buckingham to await news. Throughout the afternoon the unruffled hall-porter posted telegrams from around the country, reporting horse-race results, decisions in divorce cases, the weather, and similar matters. Meanwhile, the news machine ticked out tedious accounts of an overnight session in the House of Commons and a minor panic on the Stock Exchange. The evening newspapers arrived at four, and Lord Arthur carried the Pall Mall, the St. James's, the Globe and the Echo into the library. This greatly annoyed Colonel Goodchild, who wanted to read reports of the speech he had given that morning at the Mansion House. He had spoken about missions in South Africa and the benefits of appointing black bishops in every province, and for some reason he strongly disliked the Evening News. But none of the papers made even a passing mention of Chichester, and Lord Arthur concluded that his attempt had failed. This was a dreadful blow, and for a while he felt completely shaken. The next day he visited Herr Winckelkopf, who apologized at length and offered him a replacement clock for nothing, or a case of nitroglycerine bombs at cost. Lord Arthur, however, had lost all confidence in explosives. Herr Winckelkopf himself admitted that nowadays so many things were mixed with inferior ingredients that even pure dynamite was hard to obtain. Though the little German agreed that something must have failed in the mechanism, he still hoped the clock might explode. He gave the example of a barometer he had once sent to the military Governor of Odessa. It was set to explode after ten days, but had waited something like three months. Admittedly, when it finally went off, it had only blown a housemaid to pieces, since the Governor had left town six weeks earlier. Still, the incident at least proved that dynamite controlled by machinery was a powerful instrument of destruction, even if its punctuality left something to be desired.

“Upon that subject, then, I shall maintain a constant silence; and rest assured that, once we are married, no unkind reproach will ever escape my lips.”

It had now become quite essential to break in upon him.

“You proceed too quickly, sir,” she exclaimed. “You overlook the fact that I have not answered you. Allow me to do so without wasting another moment. Pray accept my gratitude for the compliment you offer me. I fully appreciate the honour of your proposal, but I can do nothing except refuse it.”

“I do not require to be told,” returned Mr. Collins, waving his hand ceremoniously, “that young ladies commonly refuse the attentions of a gentleman they privately intend to accept when he first solicits their favour; indeed, the refusal may sometimes be given twice, or even three times. What you have just said, therefore, does not discourage me in the least, and I shall look forward to conducting you to the altar before long.”

“Indeed, sir,” Elizabeth cried, “after my declaration, yours is a most remarkable expectation. Let me assure you that I am not among those young ladies, if any such exist, who venture to stake their happiness upon the prospect of a second offer. My refusal is entirely in earnest. You could never render me happy, and I feel certain that no woman in the world is less likely than I to render you so. Indeed, if your friend Lady Catherine were acquainted with me, I am convinced she would consider me unsuited to the position in every particular.”

“If one could be certain that Lady Catherine would hold that opinion,” said Mr. Collins with great solemnity—“but I cannot conceive that her Ladyship could disapprove of you at all. You may depend upon my speaking most highly of your modesty, thrift, and other pleasing qualities when next I have the honour of attending her.”

“Truly, Mr. Collins, there is no need to praise me. You must permit me to make my own judgment, and do me the courtesy of crediting my words. I wish you every happiness and great wealth; in declining your hand, I am doing whatever I can to ensure that neither fails you. By offering it, you must have met every obligation suggested by your delicate feelings towards my family, and you may inherit Longbourn whenever it devolves upon you without reproaching yourself. We may consequently regard this business as settled for good.” She rose while speaking, and would have left the room if Mr. Collins had not addressed her again.

“When next I permit myself the honour of discussing this matter with you, I shall trust to obtain a more encouraging reply than today's. Yet I am very far from charging you with cruelty now, for I understand that your sex customarily refuses a gentleman upon his first application; and perhaps even at present you have expressed as much encouragement of my addresses as the proper delicacy of a woman's character allows.”
